presenterNotes: Start by reviewing graphing lines in slope-intercept form, as this is essential for solving systems graphically.
Emphasize that the intersection point is the only ordered pair that satisfies both equations. Use the 'two locks, one key' analogy.
When checking a solution, insist that students substitute into the original equations, not the rewritten forms, to catch any rearrangement errors.
For real-life problems, guide students in defining variables and setting up equations. The verbal model approach is helpful.

confusionCorner.body: A common mistake is to check only one equation. A point must satisfy [[imp:all equations]] in the system to be a solution. Even if one works, the point is not a solution if another fails.
confusionCorner.title: Both Must Be True

explanation: A [[kw:system of linear equations]] is a set of two or more linear equations in the same variables.
A [[kw:solution of a system]] is an ordered pair $(x, y)$ that makes [[imp:all equations]] true.
To check if a point is a solution, substitute the $x$ and $y$ values into each equation.
If the point satisfies every equation, it is a solution. If it fails even one, it is not.

formulaCard.title: Solving by Graphing

explanation: To solve a system by graphing, graph both equations on the [[imp:same coordinate plane]].
The solution is the [[imp:point of intersection]] of the graphs.
Estimate the coordinates of the intersection point.
Check the estimated solution by substituting into both original equations.
If the lines are parallel, there is no solution. If they are the same line, there are infinitely many solutions.

confusionCorner.body: Graphing gives an estimate. The intersection may be at fractional coordinates that are hard to read precisely. Always substitute back to confirm your estimate is exact. If not, you may need to solve algebraically.
confusionCorner.title: Estimate vs. Exact

discoveryHook.scenario: Two lines on a graph represent two relationships. Their intersection point is the one pair of x and y that works for both—like two friends meeting at the same time and place. Graphing lets you see the solution immediately!

explanation: Many real-world problems involve two unknowns and two conditions, leading to a system of linear equations.

steps: Let x = min on elliptical, y = min on bike.
Solve: from first, y = 40 - x. Substitute: 8x + 6(40-x) = 300 → 8x + 240 - 6x = 300 → 2x = 60 → x=30, y=10.

formulaCard.title: Solution by Slope-Intercept Comparison
notes: $m_1 = m_2, b_1 = b_2$ → infinitely many solutions.
formulaCard.formula: $$ y = m_1x + b_1, \quad y = m_2x + b_2 $$

explanation: If the graphs of the two equations are [[imp:parallel lines]], the system has [[imp:no solution]]. (Slopes are equal, y-intercepts are different.)
If the graphs are the [[imp:same line]], the system has [[imp:infinitely many solutions]]. (Equations are equivalent.)
If the graphs intersect at one point, the system has [[imp:exactly one solution]].
You can identify these cases by comparing slopes and y-intercepts after writing both equations in slope-intercept form.

blocks.title: Special Cases: Parallel and Same Lines
teacherCues: Graph y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x - 3. Ask: 'Do these lines intersect? What does that mean for the system?'

discoveryHook.scenario: Some systems have no solution—like parallel lines that never meet. Others have infinitely many solutions—when the two equations actually describe the same line. Recognizing these special cases saves you from endless searching!

confusionCorner.title: No Solution vs. Infinite Solutions
confusionCorner.body: Parallel lines have the same slope but different y-intercepts — no intersection. The same line has both identical slope and y-intercept — every point is a solution.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Solving Systems by Graphing

explanation: The blueprint for systems: [[imp:Understand]] – Identify the unknowns, define variables, and write the two equations.
[[imp:Solve]] – Graph both lines on the same coordinate plane. Find the intersection point. Check the solution in both equations.
[[imp:Conclude]] – State the solution as an ordered pair. Interpret what it means in context. Check if the answer is reasonable.

notes: Always graph in slope-intercept form for accuracy.
If lines don't intersect or are identical, note special cases.
formulaCard.title: System Solving Blueprint

rows.1: Define variables; write equations from the problem.
Graph both lines; locate intersection; check algebraically.
State the ordered pair; answer in context; check reasonableness.

examples.title: A – Full Blueprint: Candle Sales
steps: Understand: Let x = small, y = large. Equations: x + y = 28; 4x + 6y = 144.
Solve: Graph both. Intersection at (12, 16). Check: 12+16=28, 4(12)+6(16)=48+96=144.
Conclude: 12 small candles and 16 large candles.
